newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary interior minister says bombing wave on wane.
newsitem.headline: Hungary interior minister says bombing wave on wane.

text.p: Hungarian Interior Minister Gabor Kuncze said that after a major shake-up police are dealing more effectively with a wave of bombings and shootings that has rocked Budapest.

"I am absolutely convinced we will stop it," Kuncze told Reuters in an interview. "The investigation of these cases is being carried out by a large force of police...and this will act as a kind of restraining force."
At least three people have been killed in the spate of bombings and shootings that began last September, many of them targeted at the city's nightspots, bars and car dealerships.
Two women were killed when a hand grenade exploded in the toilet of a Chinese restaurant in January and a known gangland figure was shot dead at the wheel of his car in November.

On Friday, police reported that a vagrant had been shot and critically wounded and a cook working in a restaurant was wounded by a shot fired through the window -- both with the same gun by an unknown assailant.

Kuncze, who sacked the national and Budapest police chiefs last year and has ordered a major reorganisation of the police, said the violence last year was the result of a gang war while the more recent cases usually arose from personal vendettas.
"It seems the first series was part of a battle for redistribution of the market," he said. "...There is no one behind the second wave -- these are single cases with single perpetrators."
He also maintained Budapest was still safer than many other cities.
"Let me just remind you there was that bombing at the Olympics in Atlanta and they still have not found the criminal," he said. "There are bombings in Paris and letter bombs in Austria."

But he admitted there had been significantly more bombings and shootings in Budapest in the past six months than in any other comparable period in the last five years. He blamed this in part on changes following the collapse of communism and an influx of arms to Hungary from the wars in former Yugoslavia.
"There was a new phenomenon appeared in crime in Hungary after 1990 and this includes bombings and shootouts," he said.

"And of course the entire issue is related to the fact that with the wars south of the border, a great many arms were smuggled into the country and the police have yet to find a method where they can take an efficient stand against such new phenomenon."
He said the police also suffered from internal problems, including poor organisation, financial management and discipline.
"The police force was in a condition that made it very difficult to stand up to the task of producing results when faced with such a series of criminal actions," he said.

"It is a very expressly defined requirement of the new police management that they should clean the police forces of those who should not be there, of those who may be corrupt or those who may cooperate with criminals."
One senior Western diplomat said that until recently, Hungary had not dealt with the problem effectively.

"There was too much division of attention on this issue -- the city was looking at it from its point of view, the national government from its point of view and they weren't talking to one another," the diplomat said.
"Now they are beginning to understand that this is a common problem in a not very large country and they have to work together."
